kept.title: With a preview current, its markdown buffer is Session's active buffer, and most editing paths miss a key-level gate
kept.detail:
ADR-0043 doesn't say what Session's active buffer is while a preview tab is current. Under ADR-0038 §2 and `enter/1` it becomes the preview's buffer. So everything that acts on "the active buffer" reaches a buffer the user can only see as the rendered file on disk. "Keys that would edit show a hint" doesn't say where that check sits or what counts as an edit.

The check can't live only in `apply_editor_key/2`. The typed verbs and the palette reach `apply_action/4` through `apply_verb/2` without passing through it, and paste, cut, undo, redo, revert, revert-call, select, select all, fast-forward and save are all palette entries. Grid's `cut` reaches `do_cut/2` through `do_grid/2`. `replace_selection/3` applies a running `|cmd` whenever the active buffer is still the one the command started on, which stays true while that buffer's preview is current.

It can't live only in `apply_action/4` either. `apply_key/4` dispatches `{:edit, …}` and opens `:grid` before it ever reaches `apply_action/4`.

The code's own vocabulary also leaves gaps. Undo/redo are "history operations, not edits" and save is "an operation, not an edit". A gate on edits alone would let Alt+Z / Alt+Shift+Z change the buffer where the user can't see it. It would also let Alt+U / `revert-call` take back the change on Session's cursor line, a line the preview neither shows nor marks.

The Consequences say "the editing path doesn't change" and "the preview never edits". Neither holds without a check placed in that path.

kept.amendment:
Add to §1, and amend ADR-0038 §2:

"While a preview is current, its buffer is Session's active buffer. One predicate, 'the current tab is a preview', is checked where actions come in: in `apply_editor_key/2` before `Keymap.resolve/3`, in `apply_verb/2` (the typed verbs and the palette), and in `run_pipe/2` and `replace_selection/3`.

Allowed in a preview: the scroll keys (arrows, Alt+W/S, Home/End, Page Up/Down), Alt+M, Alt+I, Alt+P/O/K/T/L/Y, Alt+1–9 / , / . / - / =, Alt+Shift+P, Ctrl-X/Q/C, and the verbs open, find, buffers, close, preview, tab, split, vsplit, theme, mouse, new, mkdir, rename, delete and `!`.

Everything else shows the hint: typing and every edit key, paste, cut, copy, selection, undo, redo, revert, revert-call, Alt+G and its verbs, `line N`, and `|`."

Decide Ctrl-O and Alt+J explicitly; neither needs a cursor.

check.reason:
The gap is real. enter/1 (loop.ex:954-958) makes the current tab's buffer Session's active buffer, whatever kind of tab it is. ADR-0038 §2 (lines 40-44) keeps it that way, and ADR-0043 §1 doesn't override it. apply_key/4 handles {:edit,…}, :grid and :palette itself, before apply_action/4 (loop.ex:3545-3589). Typed verbs and the palette reach apply_action/4 through apply_verb/2 (4271, 4318, 4419) and never pass apply_editor_key/2. The palette offers paste, undo, redo, revert, revert-call, fast-forward, highlight, select all and save (catalog.ex:38-55, 148-172). do_revert/3 acts on Session's cursor line (4018-4020). replace_selection/3 checks only the active buffer and its text (2937-2944). keymap.ex:121 and :166 call undo/redo and save 'not edits'. So 'keys that would edit show a hint' leaves the palette and the verbs open, and doesn't classify undo, redo or revert.

Overstated in three ways:
- The ADR opens the preview beside its source, so the buffer's text is normally visible in the other pane. It is not 'only the rendered file'.
- The Consequences' 'editing path' means the shared path, provenance, undo and replay. A gate in the loop doesn't touch them; only 'the preview never edits' depends on the gate.
- High is closer to medium.

The amendment is wrong in two places. First, its gate points miss two paths: `line N` (submit_minibuffer's {:line, n} → jump_to_line/2, loop.ex:4262 and 4377, which doesn't go through apply_verb/2) and the mouse press (press/4 → select_to/5 sets Session's cursor and a selection, 1159-1210). Second, its allowed verbs leave out quit/exit, tree, edits and no (verbs.ex:166, 189-190, 203-204). 'Everything else shows the hint' would then refuse `quit`, which loop.ex:4396 says must always work.

kept.title: A preview counts as another view of its buffer, so closing the last source tab skips the unsaved-edits refusal and leaves the preview behind
kept.detail:
"On the file's buffer, so closing the file closes its previews" holds only when the buffer process ends (`:DOWN` → `Panes.drop_buffer/2`). The loop's own close paths ask whether the buffer has another tab, and a preview is one:
- `do_close/1` takes the `Panes.elsewhere?/2` branch before its unsaved-edits check.
- The tab × refuses only when the buffer is dirty `and not Panes.in_other_pane?/3`.
- The pane × leaves any buffer that is `in_other_pane?` out of its own-buffers set, so neither its dirty check nor `safe_close_buffer` sees it.

So Alt+K, the source tab's ×, or the source pane's × all close the last source tab with "still open in another pane". They skip ADR-0038 §4's refusal over unsaved edits and leave the preview as the buffer's only tab.

Alt+K on that preview then runs the buffer path. It either closes the buffer (`close_active`/`safe_close_buffer`) or refuses over unsaved edits the preview can't show, and with the editing gate the user can't save or undo them from there. Reopening the file from that pane lands on the preview again (see open-reuses-preview).

Closing a preview from its source (the toggle) has no `Panes` call. `close_tab/1` closes only the current pane's shown tab, and the tab-× path first moves focus into the preview's pane and runs `do_close/1`.

kept.amendment:
Add to §1, recorded as an amendment to ADR-0038 §4:

"Only source tabs count as a buffer's views. `elsewhere?/2`, `in_other_pane?/3` and `close_pane/2`'s own-buffers set ignore previews. Closing a buffer's last source tab closes its previews with it, and is refused while the buffer has unsaved edits, as in ADR-0038 §4.

Closing a preview (Alt+K, its ×, or the toggle from either tab) removes only that tab, through a new `Panes` call that closes a given pane's tab without changing focus. It never closes the buffer and never asks about unsaved edits."

check.reason:
The close paths all count the preview as another view of the buffer:
- do_close/1 takes the Panes.elsewhere?/2 branch before its dirty check (loop.ex:3786-3792), and elsewhere?/2 counts any other tab of the buffer (panes.ex:190-198).
- The tab × refuses only when the buffer is dirty and not in_other_pane?/3 (loop.ex:1507-1521; panes.ex:154-160).
- close_pane/2's `own` set drops buffers that are in other panes before its dirty check and before safe_close_buffer (loop.ex:1531-1555).
- Only the buffer's :DOWN drops all its tabs (loop.ex:745-758).

So with the preview as a plain Panes tab on the buffer, Alt+K, the source tab's × or its pane's × closes the last source tab with 'still open in another pane'. The preview becomes the buffer's only tab. §1's 'closing the file closes its previews' therefore holds only when the buffer process ends.

The skipped refusal loses no edits by itself, since the buffer stays open. The harm is the orphaned preview. Alt+K on it runs the last-tab path (loop.ex:3796-3808) and refuses over unsaved edits the preview can't show. Opens from its pane land on it (open-reuses-preview). Whether the user is fully stuck depends on whether Ctrl-O is allowed in a preview.

Panes.close_tab/1 closes only the current pane's shown tab (panes.ex:131-143), so the toggle from the source tab needs a new call. The amendment is right.

"Only source tabs count as a buffer's views. `Panes.elsewhere?/2`, `Panes.in_other_pane?/3` and `close_pane/2`'s own-buffers set ignore previews.

Closing a buffer's last source tab (Alt+K, its ×, or its pane's ×) closes the buffer and its previews with it. It is refused while the buffer has unsaved edits, as in ADR-0038 §4.

Closing a preview (Alt+K, its ×, or the toggle from either tab) removes only that tab. It goes through a new `Panes` call that closes a given pane's tab without changing the current pane. It never closes the buffer and never asks about unsaved edits."

kept.title: Opening the file from the preview's pane shows the preview, and a jump to a line lands where there is no cursor
kept.detail:
`Panes.show/3` picks a pane's tab by buffer alone, and `adopt_active/2` returns early when the current tab's buffer is the one being opened. So in a pane where the file's tab is its preview, every open of that file shows the preview: Alt+O, the tree, `open PATH`, the buffers picker, the output pane's path:line and the edits pane's entry.

`open_entry/2` and `open_location/2` then `set_cursor` the target line into Session while the preview is current. On the next switch, `leave/1` copies that cursor into the preview tab and `enter/1` gives the source tab its old cursor back, so the jump is lost.

This is the ordinary path after reading a preview. The current pane stays the last file pane while the tree or the edits pane has focus, and the preview has to take focus to be scrolled with keys. No source tab can be added to that pane at all.

The early return can't simply be narrowed to source tabs. Entering a preview whose buffer wasn't active makes Session send `{:geex_active_buffer, pid}` to every subscriber, the loop included. That echo relies on the early return to change nothing; narrowed, it would open a source tab over the preview just entered.

kept.amendment:
Add to §1:

"The loop's own opens show the file's source tab. That covers `open_tab/2`, and with it `do_open`, the tree, the finder, `open_entry/2` and `open_location/2`, plus `pick/2` for a buffer. `Panes.show/3` matches source tabs only. In a pane where the file has only a preview, a source tab is added after the preview and shown, so a jump from the edits pane or the output pane lands on text.

`adopt_active/2`'s early return still matches any tab on the buffer, so Session's echo of a preview becoming current changes nothing."

check.reason:
The finding is real:
- Panes.show/3 picks a pane's tab by buffer alone (panes.ex:79-90).
- adopt_active/2 returns early when the current tab's buffer is the pid (loop.ex:882-885). Otherwise it shows the existing tab and restores that tab's cursor (891-899).
- open_tab/2 (931-938), pick/2 for a buffer (4288-4292), open_entry/2 (3106-3115) and open_location/2 (3004-3014) all show through adopt_active/2. The last two then set_cursor into Session.
- leave/1 copies Session's cursor into the current tab (942-946), and enter/1 restores the other tab's cursor (954-962), so the jump is lost.
- The current pane stays the preview's pane while the tree or the edits pane has focus (panes.ex:10-11).

The echo argument also holds. put_active/2 sends {:geex_active_buffer, pid} to every subscriber (session.ex:577-588), and the loop handles it with adopt_active/2 (loop.ex:414-415). Narrowing the early return would open a source tab over a preview just entered.

The amendment, though, is inconsistent as written. It keeps adopt_active/2's any-tab early return, yet it names open_tab/2 and pick/2, which reach the show step only through adopt_active/2. In the main case, where the preview is the current tab, that early return fires and the open still lands on the preview. The opens have to show the source tab themselves.
check.amendment:
Add to §1:

"The loop's own opens show the file's source tab. `open_tab/2` (and with it `do_open`, the tree, the finder, `open_entry/2` and `open_location/2`) and `pick/2` for a buffer show it themselves, through a `Panes.show/3` that matches source tabs only. They don't go through `adopt_active/2`, whose early return fires exactly when the file's preview is the current tab.

In a pane where the file has only a preview, a source tab is added at the end of the pane's tabs and shown, so a jump from the edits pane or the output pane lands on text.

`adopt_active/2` handles Session's `{:geex_active_buffer, pid}`. It keeps its early return for any tab on that buffer, so Session's echo of a preview becoming current changes nothing."

kept.title: "No cursor" conflicts with a tab type, and loop code, that require and pass along cursor, hscroll and hold
kept.detail:
A `Panes` tab is `%{buffer, cursor, scroll, hscroll, hold}`, and the loop reads or updates those fields on every tab it shows or makes current.

If a preview lacks the fields, the loop crashes on the first frame after the preview opens. `pane_view/5` reads `tab.cursor` for the non-current pane, a KeyError. `enter/1`'s `case` has no clause for a map without `:cursor`. `leave/1`, `apply_editor_key/2` and `hold_scroll/5` update with `%{tab | …}`. The loop is a permanent child, so after the crash it restarts with `new_state/2`'s single fresh pane.

If a preview keeps the fields, they hold source coordinates that leak. `enter/1` sets Session's cursor to the preview's, and `leave/1` and `draw_pane/6` write Session's cursor back into it. Session's `put_active/2` stores whatever cursor it holds as the buffer's last cursor, and `adopt_active/2` gives that cursor to the file's next new source tab.

A round trip source → preview → source does keep the source tab's own cursor, because `leave/1` copies it out first. The risk is the preview's value standing in for the file's cursor, not a clobber of the source tab.

Add to §1:

"A preview tab is `%{buffer, view: :preview, scroll}`, where `scroll` counts rendered rows; it has no `cursor`, `hscroll` or `hold`. A source tab is the same map with `view: :source`.

`enter/1` makes a preview's buffer active but leaves Session's cursor alone, and `leave/1` copies nothing out of a preview. Every loop path that reads or updates a tab's cursor, hscroll or hold handles the preview first: `pane_view/5`, `draw_pane/6`, `enter/1`, `leave/1`, `adopt_active/2`, `apply_editor_key/2`, `select_to/5` and `hold_scroll/5`."

check.reason:
The code is as cited:
- The Panes tab type and tab/2 carry cursor, scroll, hscroll and hold (panes.ex:23-31, 44-47).
- pane_view/5 reads tab.cursor (loop.ex:1775-1777).
- enter/1's case matches only a map with :cursor (954-962).
- leave/1, apply_editor_key/2 and hold_scroll/5 update with %{tab | …} (942-946, 849, 1262-1270).
- draw_pane/6 writes cursor, hold and hscroll back every frame (1854-1857).
- put_active/2 remembers the view cursor as the old buffer's (session.ex:577-594), and adopt_active/2 starts a new tab from Session's cursor (loop.ex:887-897).

But the ADR does say the preview's scroll is over rendered rows and that it has no cursor. A map without those fields crashing is a build hazard the first test would catch, not a conflict in the design.

What the ADR really leaves open is what enter/1 and leave/1 do with Session's cursor for a preview. Keeping the fields leaks only cosmetically: the file's next new source tab opens at the preview's placeholder cursor instead of where the user last was. The finding itself concedes the source tab isn't clobbered. Medium is closer to low.

kept.title: §6's scroll to the saving tab's cursor needs a cursor, but the save message carries only the buffer, and the buffer never sees a cursor
kept.detail:
§6 has the preview scroll to "the block holding that tab's cursor" after a save from a tab of the same file. §2's trigger is `{:geex_buffer_saved, buffer}` from the buffer's save handler, and the preview process subscribes to the buffer. Neither knows which tab saved or where its cursor was: the cursor is view-local, kept in Session and the loop (ADR-0014 §2), never in the buffer.

Only the loop knows, at `do_save/1`. The rows come back later from a process that coalesces requests, so a reconcile change can fold into the same render.

The ADR also leaves two cases open:
- A save made from the preview itself, if Ctrl-O is allowed there, where there's no tab cursor.
- A save where `Reconcile.save` merged the disk's change in first, so the cursor's line no longer names the same text.

Rewrite §6's second rule:

"When the loop's own save (Ctrl-O, `save`) succeeds from a source tab, the loop records `{buffer, cursor line}`. When the next rows for that buffer arrive, each of its preview tabs scrolls to the block holding that line, clamped to the new text, instead of keeping its top block.

A save from a preview, or from outside the loop, keeps the reader's place."

check.reason:
Checked: §2's message is {:geex_buffer_saved, buffer} (ADR:82-84). handle_call(:save) writes the file and replies {:ok, path}, with no cursor (buffer.ex:466-477). The cursor is view-local, in Session (session.ex:7-9).

But the ADR never has the preview process do §6's scrolling, and it couldn't. A buffer may have several previews (§3), and each tab's scroll lives in the loop's Panes. The loop runs the save (do_save/1, loop.ex:3726-3746) and subscribes to every watched buffer (4453-4454), so the loop already has the cursor. The ADR also lists 'whether the preview follows the cursor on save by default' under 'To settle when built'.

The merged-first case isn't specific to the preview. The view cursor follows no outside edit anywhere: Session never subscribes to buffers, and the loop ignores the change footprint (loop.ex:434). §3 also gives rendering no correctness contract.

What's left is small: say that the loop applies the rule, and which saves count.

"The loop applies it, since it owns every preview tab's scroll and runs the save. When its own save (Ctrl-O, `save`) succeeds from a source tab, it notes `{buffer, cursor line}`. When that buffer's next rows arrive, each of its preview tabs scrolls to the block holding that line, clamped to the new text, instead of keeping its top block.

A save from a preview, or from outside the loop, keeps the reader's place. `{:geex_buffer_saved, buffer}` stays a render trigger and carries no cursor."

kept.title: The wheel, scroll bar, press and drag paths work in source lines and place a caret
kept.detail:
The ADR gives the preview "a scroll over rendered rows", moved by arrows, Page Up/Down and the wheel, and says a link click opens its target. Every existing mouse path computes against the tab's source text:
- **Wheel.** `wheel/4` → `scrolled/4` bounds the scroll by the source's line count and widest line. A short file whose paragraphs wrap into more rows than it has lines can't be wheeled to its end. A file whose link definitions render to nothing scrolls past its end. Shift+wheel sets an `hscroll` the preview doesn't have.
- **Scroll bar.** Its layout, hit test and thumb drag read the source text.
- **Press.** `press/4` sends the cell through `Mouse.text_pos/4`, which makes a caret on line `tab.scroll + row`, using a rendered-row index as a source line. `select_to/5` then sets Session's cursor and a selection, and `start_drag/3` begins a drag that selects text. A double-click selects a source word; Shift/Alt+press extends the selection.
- **Drawing.** `draw_pane/6` scrolls to keep the cursor's line in view.

ADR-0039 §3 and §7 (a press places the cursor; the bars are laid out from the text) still govern a preview unless amended. The Consequences' "it addresses nothing" fails while a press turns a cell into a caret.

kept.title: A rename re-keys the buffer without telling its subscribers, so the preview's path and whether it applies go stale

kept.adr_section: §2 It shows the file on disk
kept.detail: The preview reads the file, but a buffer can have a path with no file behind it. kept.title: Who owns, supervises and stops the preview process is left open, and the obvious choices break 'a crash costs a frame'
kept.detail: The model §3 names, Highlight.Reactor, is started by Session.open_file under ReactorSupervisor. It is registered as {:highlight_reactor, buffer}, monitors its buffer, and lives exactly as long as the buffer; the loop never counts or stops it. The preview instead 'starts with a buffer's first preview and stops with its last'. Only the loop's Panes, which is pure state inside the loop, can keep that count. The loop is a permanent child. If it crashes, it restarts with fresh panes and no preview tabs. A preview process stopped only by the old count then lives until its buffer closes, re-reading and re-parsing on every save (0.45–0.7 s for testing.md) for nobody. The reactor drops a dead subscriber but never stops for lack of one, so copying it doesn't fix this. If a later Alt+Shift+P registers per buffer, it meets {:already_started, pid}. 'In a task' read as Task.async links the task to the process, so one parse or layout crash kills the :temporary preview process for good; the reactor uses spawn plus monitor. The loop doesn't monitor reactors today. A dead preview process would leave its tab frozen on stale rows with no notice, against ADR-0035 §1. The new process is also a buffer subscriber. It receives `{:geex_buffer_change, …}` on every keystroke and the opened notice the moment it subscribes, and the reactor's catch-all exists because lacking one crashed it. Existing subscribers (the loop and the reactor) do tolerate the new message: both have catch-alls.

kept.title: 'Keeps only the latest request' would let a width change replace a pending save's re-read
kept.detail: The reactor can keep a single boolean `pending` because it has one kind of request: highlight the newest text. The preview has at least three kinds, which §2 and §6 keep apart: re-read the file (on open, save, or behind), re-lay out the last parse (a width change, 'without reading the file'), and scroll to the saving tab's cursor (§6). Taken literally, 'keeps only the latest request' drops the save. Suppose a save arrives while a long render is running (0.45–0.7 s on testing.md), and a resize or split drag comes before that render ends. The width request replaces the save's re-read, so only the old parse is laid out again. The saved text doesn't show until the next save or behind change, and showing it is what the preview is for.

kept.title: §2's width re-layout says neither where it runs nor how widths reach a per-buffer process; laying out testing.md measures about 100 ms
kept.detail: §2 says a changed width 'lays the last parse out again, without reading the file', but not who does it. The last parse lives in the preview process, where the parse ran. The width lives in the loop and changes per pane: on every terminal resize, and on every motion event while a split or the tree is dragged. Measured here with the spike, Layout.rows alone on doc/testing.md takes about 90–113 ms (4,735 rows at 100 columns, 6,866 at 60). The tree it needs is 2.6 MB. Run in the loop, it would stall typing at every resize step (ADR-0035 §1). One process per buffer can also be asked for several widths at once. A tab belongs to one pane, the same buffer can be a tab in two panes of different widths, and §3's 'first preview … last' assumes several previews per buffer. The build has to decide how the loop gives the process each tab's width, whether rows are kept per width, and how arriving rows are matched to a tab, since under ADR-0035 a superseded answer must be ignored. Pushing the whole row list to the loop is not the problem: 1.6 MB of rows for testing.md took about 1 ms to send between processes.

kept.title: A fast-forward that takes in a change before the watcher reports it sends nothing the preview hears
kept.detail: Under ADR-0034 §3, Ctrl-O reads the disk and fast-forwards first, 'whether or not the watcher has noticed the change yet'. That fast-forward moves `synced` to the new disk text. Its only announcement is `caught_up` → `set_behind(nil)`, which is silent when no mark was set. If the merge leaves conflicts, a leftover marker block refuses the write, or the write errors, no save follows, so there is no `{:geex_buffer_saved, …}` either. When the watcher reports a moment later, the disk equals the new `synced`, the mark stays nil and `set_behind` skips the repeat. The preview keeps showing the version from before the agent's write while the disk holds the agent's, and the header has no 'behind'. The same happens when Alt+J is pressed before the report. It happens for every agent write when the watcher is degraded (no inotify-tools), because then only the fast-forward and the save ever read the disk.

The preview re-renders on that message and on `{:geex_buffer_behind, …}`. Consequences can still say the buffer sends one new message.

A save fast-forwards first, and a merge with conflicts returns without writing (reconcile.ex:196-201); a leftover marker block refuses the write (reconcile.ex:204-217). When the watcher reports later, the disk equals the new synced, so behind stays nil and set_behind skips the repeat (buffer.ex:412-421, 611). Alt+J (loop.ex:3828) takes the same path. So after a fast-forward that doesn't end in a successful save, the preview never re-reads. It shows the pre-agent text with no 'behind', against §2's promise (85-88). The only message sent is {:geex_buffer_change}, which the preview ignores because it isn't live. A clean merge on Ctrl-O does write, and the save message covers that case, so the gap is conflicts, refusals, write errors and Alt+J. `synced` moves only at three places: save (buffer.ex:470), a group with a baseline, and mark_synced (buffer.ex:441, no caller in lib/). Those are exactly the amendment's three sites.

The preview re-renders on that message and on `{:geex_buffer_behind, …}`, and skips the read when the hash is the one it last rendered. Consequences can still say the buffer sends one new message.

kept.title: The preview's read can catch the buffer's in-place write half done, and a rewrite with identical bytes never corrects it
kept.detail: Buffer.save writes with File.write, which truncates the file and rewrites it in place. On Ctrl-O while behind, the fast-forward's `caught_up` sends `{:geex_buffer_behind, buffer, nil}`, and a few calls later Buffer.save truncates and rewrites the file. The render that message starts reads at the same time as the write, so it can parse an empty or truncated file. The save message that follows does re-render. But in the reactor's shape every finished pass is published, even when a newer one is pending, so the truncated render is drawn first. And when §6 isn't anchoring to a cursor, it takes the reader's place from that truncated render. The watcher's 50 ms settle protects only the watcher's own read. A partial read made while some other writer rewrites the file with the same bytes (a formatter, a checkout of the same blob) is never corrected at all: the same sha256 keeps `behind` as it was, a disk equal to `synced` stays nil, and set_behind skips repeats.

kept.amendment: Add to §3: "Each trigger names the bytes it expects: behind's sha256, or the sha256 the buffer wrote, carried by its save (or synced) message. The preview draws a read only when its sha256 matches the newest expected hash. Otherwise it reads again after the reconcile settle (50 ms), and after three tries draws what it has with the header saying the file is changing. A render overtaken by a newer trigger before it finishes isn't drawn, and §6 takes its place from the last render drawn."

check.reason: The cited code checks out. buffer.ex:468 writes in place with File.write, which truncates and then writes. On Ctrl-O while behind, caught_up sends behind=nil (buffer.ex:605-607, 613-614) before reconcile.ex:205-209 reaches Buffer.save. The reactor publishes a finished pass before starting the pending one (reactor.ex:269-293). The settle covers only the watcher's read (reconcile.ex:410-415). Identical bytes send nothing (buffer.ex:415-416, 611). But the race is narrow. It needs no render in flight and a preview read that lands inside the microseconds of the write. Usually the loop's get_text and marker scan (reconcile.ex:205) let the read finish first, and the save's own re-render follows. The never-corrected case needs a same-bytes rewrite by another writer to coincide with a preview read. §3 already says rendering has no correctness contract. The amendment has two flaws. First, 'a render overtaken by a newer trigger isn't drawn' would freeze the view while an agent writes a large file faster than one render (0.45–0.7 s, §8); the reactor publishes every pass for that reason. Second, a behind=nil message carries no hash, so the synced hash has to come from the save (synced) message or from the buffer.
check.amendment: Add to §3: "The preview draws a read only when its sha256 is the hash the buffer last gave for the disk: behind's sha256 while behind, otherwise the synced text's. The synced hash comes from the buffer's save (synced) message, or from the buffer when the preview opens; a behind=nil message carries none. On a mismatch it reads again after the reconcile settle (50 ms). After three tries it draws what it read and the header says the file is changing. Renders that pass the check are drawn as they finish, even with a newer one pending, so an agent writing a large file faster than one render takes can't freeze the view."

kept.title: `{:geex_buffer_saved, buffer}` can't tell §6 that the user saved, or where their cursor was
kept.detail: §6 scrolls to the saving tab's cursor 'when the user saved from a tab of the same file'. The message names neither who saved nor a cursor, and it reaches the preview process straight from the buffer. Every save sends it: the loop's Ctrl-O (Reconcile.save/2), and an agent's MCP `save_file`, which calls Buffer.save/1 on the active buffer. Built on the message alone, an agent's save would jump the human's preview to the human's cursor. The cursor is view-local: in Session for the current tab, in Panes for every other tab. Only the loop knows its own save succeeded and which tab's cursor applies. And because renders coalesce, the first render to land after a save may have started before it.

doc/adr/0043-markdown-preview.md:163-164 — "When the user saved from a tab of the same file, the preview scrolls instead to the block holding that tab's cursor"

lib/geex/loop.ex:3726-3731 — do_save: `Reconcile.save(&1, …)` returns `{:ok, path}` to the loop
lib/geex/buffer.ex:26-27 and lib/geex/loop/panes.ex:12-15 — the cursor is view-local, not in the buffer

The process keeps it with the pending request and applies it to the first render it starts afterwards. The buffer's save message, which an agent's MCP save_file also sends, is a plain re-render that keeps the reader's place."

check.reason: The gap is real. The message is {:geex_buffer_saved, buffer} (ADR-0043:83), but §6 (163-164) needs the saving tab's cursor. The cursor is view-local, not in the buffer (buffer.ex:26-27, panes.ex:12-15). Only the loop's do_save sees {:ok, path} come back from Reconcile.save (loop.ex:3726-3731). So the message alone can't set §6's anchor; the loop has to supply it. The failure scenario can't happen, though. MCP save_file (operations.ex:177-187) runs only under geex.serve: config/runtime.exs sets start_http_mcp: true and start_terminal: false together, so no loop or preview exists then. Reconcile.save and fast_forward have no caller but the loop (loop.ex:3728, 3828). Every save a preview can see is the loop's own Ctrl-O. The amendment's design is sound: the loop sends the cursor line, and the process attaches it to the first render started afterwards, which also handles coalescing. Only its MCP rationale is wrong.
check.amendment: Add to §6: "The anchor comes from the loop, not from the buffer's message. While a preview can be open, the loop's own Ctrl-O is the only save: MCP's save_file runs only under geex.serve, where there is no terminal. When do_save gets {:ok, _}, the loop sends the buffer's preview process the saving tab's cursor line. The process attaches it to the first render it starts afterwards, and the loop scrolls those rows to the block holding that line. The buffer's save message is a plain re-render that keeps the reader's place."

kept.title: Rows carry code colours already resolved against the theme, so a theme change is a trigger §2–3 leave out
kept.detail: §5 says Style turns roles into colours at draw time, 'so the layout never sees a theme'. In the spike, fenced code is coloured during layout. Layout.rows's :code callback returns `%{byte => Geex.Theme.Style.t()}`, mix geex.render builds those styles with `Highlight.Paint.styles(theme, spans)`, the runs carry `{:style, style}`, and Style applies them as they are. Built that way, the preview process needs the theme as an input. A theme change leaves fenced code in the old theme's colours while everything else recolours, until the next save or behind change. Theme changes include `theme NAME`, picking or merely previewing a theme in Alt+Y, a theme update, and the terminal theme's answer to OSC 11. None of these is among §2's triggers.

Layout's :code callback returns %{byte => Theme.Style} (layout.ex:57-59), and code runs become {seg, [:code_block, {:style, style}]} (layout.ex:273-281). mix geex.render's callback closes over the theme through Paint.styles (geex.render.ex:97, 115-128), and Style applies the resolved style as given (style.ex:56). The loop changes theme on the OSC 11 answer (loop.ex:629), the Alt+Y preview (2376), `theme NAME` (3711) and a theme update (617-618). Built like the spike, the preview leaves fenced code in the old theme's colours after any of these, and §2–3 list no such trigger. §4 itself says code goes 'through the same NIF and theme as the editor'. Calling it a 'false claim' is overstated: Layout.rows never receives a theme, only a callback. What's false is that the rows it returns are theme-free. The main amendment is also lossy, because which capture wins a byte depends on the theme. Paint.styles drops spans the theme doesn't style, then lets the narrowest win (paint.ex:27-40), and Theme.style_for falls back by prefix and returns nil when nothing matches (theme.ex:56-67). With one {:capture, name} per run, a run whose narrowest capture the theme doesn't style would show the default colour where a wider styled capture should show.

At draw time `Geex.Markdown.Style` takes the first one the theme styles, which matches `Highlight.Paint.styles/2`. So neither the layout nor the preview process sees a theme, and a theme change needs no re-render." If the spike's `{:style, s}` runs are kept instead, add a theme change to §2's triggers, as a re-layout of the last parse: `theme NAME`, the Alt+Y preview or choice, a theme update, or the terminal theme's OSC 11 answer.

kept.title: A rename tells subscribers nothing, so a preview that keeps its path (as the reactor keeps its language) reads the old file
kept.adr_section: §1 Which files; §3 Off the key loop
kept.detail: Buffer.rename changes the buffer's path and sends no message. The reactor, the model §3 names, takes its language from the path once at start, and Session.rekey_buffer restarts it through Reactor.rewatch. Nothing does the same for a preview. A preview process handed the path at start would read the old path (`:enoent`) on every render after a rename. Renames come from the `rename` verb, the tree's `r`, and an agent's MCP `rename_file`, all through Session.rename_file. §1 also doesn't say whether a preview stays open when the file is renamed to a name that isn't markdown.

The reactor fixes its language from the path at start (reactor.ex:141-150, 186-188). The `rename` verb and the tree's `r` go through Session.rename_file (file_ops.ex:167-168), and so does MCP rename_file (operations.ex:212-213), though MCP runs only headless. ADR-0043 never says how the preview process learns the path. Unlike the reactor, which reads text from the buffer (reactor.ex:407-412), the preview reads the file. A path kept from start would therefore read the old, moved-away path (:enoent) after every rename, and nothing in existing code would tell it. Buffer.status/1 is a cheap call (buffer.ex:432-433) that also returns dirty and behind, which §2's header needs. The amendment is cheap and correct.

A preview stays open across a rename whatever the new name, and closes with its buffer or with Alt+Shift+P."

kept.title: A preview tab on the file's buffer keeps the buffer open: Alt+K, a tab's × and a pane's × no longer close the file or refuse its unsaved edits
kept.detail: §1 says a preview is a tab "on the file's buffer, so closing the file closes its previews". To Loop.Panes a preview is then just another tab of that buffer, and every close path asks Panes whether the buffer is in another tab. do_close/1 (Alt+K, and a tab's × after it switches to the tab) closes only the tab and keeps the buffer "still open in another pane" whenever Panes.elsewhere?/2 is true, a branch taken before the unsaved-edits refusal. A tab's × refuses unsaved edits only when the buffer is not in another pane (Panes.in_other_pane?/3). A pane's × leaves out of `own` every buffer another pane has, so it neither refuses nor closes that buffer. So closing the source tab or the source pane leaves the buffer, unsaved edits included, behind a read-only tab that shows the disk. Previews close only when the buffer process ends (the :DOWN handler's Panes.drop_buffer/2), which none of these paths causes. It gets worse. Panes.show/3 finds a pane's tab by buffer alone, adopt_active/2 returns early when the current tab's buffer is the one opened, and Session.open_file/1 returns the buffer already open. So opening the file again from the preview's pane (Alt+O, the tree, the edits list, `open PATH`, an agent's open_file) shows the preview instead of an editing tab, and the only way back to editing is to close the preview first. ADR-0038 §4's "a buffer still in another tab or pane stays open" is the rule doing this.

Closing a preview tab (Alt+K, its ×, Alt+Shift+P) closes only that tab, never the buffer." Record this as an amendment to ADR-0038 §4.

check.reason: Every cited line says what the finding claims. Panes.show/3 finds a tab by its buffer alone (lib/geex/loop/panes.ex:82). in_other_pane?/3 (panes.ex:154-160) and elsewhere?/2 (panes.ex:190-198) count any tab of the buffer. do_close/1 tests Panes.elsewhere? before the unsaved-edits check (lib/geex/loop.ex:3786-3792), so Alt+K on the source, with a preview tab of the same buffer in another pane, closes only the tab ("still open in another pane") and never refuses. A tab's x refuses only when the buffer is in no other pane, then calls do_close (loop.ex:1507-1521). close_pane leaves out of `own` every buffer another pane holds, so it neither refuses nor closes it (loop.ex:1534-1555). safe_close_buffer runs only in do_close's last branch, which is never reached while another tab holds the buffer. Tabs are otherwise dropped only on the buffer's :DOWN (loop.ex:745-758). Session.open_file returns the buffer already open, and put_active does nothing when that buffer is already active (lib/geex/session.ex:271-279, 488-500, 577-589). adopt_active returns early when the current tab's buffer is that pid (loop.ex:884-885), and otherwise calls Panes.show (897), which would find the preview tab. If the buffer is dirty and only the preview is left, Alt+K on the preview is refused too. ADR-0043 changes none of these rules.

kept.title: "The other pane" isn't defined beyond one pane, and Panes.split/2 neither takes the preview tab nor leaves focus on the source
kept.detail: Panes.split/2 gives the new pane a copy of the current tab and makes that pane current (the loop's split/2 then enters it). Opening a preview tab in a new pane while the source keeps focus therefore needs a split call that takes the new pane's tab and doesn't move focus. Panes has no idea of an "other" pane, only reading order (ids/1), so with three or more panes, or two stacked, the build has to choose where the preview goes. The loop refuses a split whose half would be under 12 columns ("no room to split this pane"), so the Consequences' "on a narrow terminal the preview takes the other half like any split" doesn't always hold, and the ADR doesn't say what the key does then. When the preview closes, its pane shows the tab before it in the list (Panes.close_tab/1), not the tab it showed before the preview: a pane that showed A of [A, B, C] comes back showing C. Alt+-/Alt+= on a preview tab copies it into a second preview of the file, and "pressed again … it closes the preview" doesn't say which one. Finally, "a click on a relative link opens its target in the source pane" needs the preview to know its source pane, and no Panes tab records one.

kept.title: The "keys that would edit show a hint" rule misses typed verbs and the palette, which edit the previewed file through Session
kept.detail: Session's active buffer is the current pane's shown tab (ADR-0038 §2). With a preview current, that is the previewed file, at whatever cursor the preview tab carries. Typed verbs and palette picks don't go through the keymap: submit_minibuffer/1 and dispatch_palette/2 call apply_verb/2, which runs apply_action/4 with Session's snapshot. So `paste`, `cut`, `undo`, `redo`, `revert`, `revert-call`, `highlight`, `select all`, `| cmd` and `line N` act on the file from a tab that shows neither a cursor nor the change, while the same chords show the hint. That breaks the ADR-0028 parity the loop is built on ("copy and Alt+C converge on one code path"). Typed edits arrive from the keymap as {:edit, …} and grid mode as :grid; both are handled in apply_key/4, outside apply_action/4, so a refusal placed in only one of the two misses the other door. The ADR also doesn't say whether save (Ctrl-O) and fast-forward (Alt+J) work from the preview, though §2 points the reader to Alt+J when the header says "behind".

kept.title: TabBar.layout/5 has no way to place or find the glyph, and a preview tab's label is undefined

kept.title: Code-block highlighting puts theme colours into Layout's rows, so §5's theme-free layout and §2's cheap re-layout don't hold

kept.detail: §5 says Style turns roles into colours when drawing, 'so the layout never sees a theme'. §2 says a width change lays the last parse out again without reading the file. kept.title: An empty `||` cell is dropped, so the rest of the row draws under the wrong headers
kept.detail: Layout treats a row's cells as its table_cell children, by position, padded or cut to the header's count. The block grammar has no cell for an empty `||`. Header-only tables also render right, and so do rows with more cells than the header (the extras are dropped, as GFM does).
